Threat.value: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
I feel on guard even inside my own home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it
Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind.

vignette: Mrs. Lin, a 76-year-old South Eastern Asian woman, has been married for over five decades and works as a mechanic in her community garage. Her life took an ominous turn several months ago when she became the target of relentless stalking by an unknown individual. The trauma of this experience has left indelible marks on her daily existence, manifesting through various symptoms that have progressively worsened. The initial incident occurred while Mrs. Lin was walking home from work one evening. She noticed a man following her and managed to escape into her house, but the fear lingered. Since then, she has been plagued by vivid memories of the stalking episode, often triggered by seemingly benign stimuli such as the scent of soil or fresh air that reminds her of the outdoors where it all began. These triggers not only evoke powerful recollections but also leave her feeling disoriented and unable to articulate what happened clearly. Whenever Mrs. Lin tries to recount the experience to family or friends, she finds herself losing the thread of her narrative, unable to fully convey the intensity of those moments. This inability to explain what transpired often leaves her frustrated and withdrawn from social interactions. Her memories are fragmented but detailed; at times, they feel as if she is reliving the event through a series of snapshots in her mind. The scent of soil or outdoor smells can instantly transport Mrs. Lin back to that terrifying evening, causing her to become hypervigilant and on high alert. She frequently looks behind her while walking home from work, convinced that the stalker might be following her once again. Her heightened sense of threat is further exacerbated by the fact that she feels equally unsafe even inside her own home. The memory of the event, with its photographic clarity, reinforces this hypervigilance and makes her wary of any sign of intrusion. Mrs. Lin’s memories of the stalking incident are not only vivid but also intrusive. They often resurface unbidden during moments when she feels happy or relaxed, disrupting her sense of peace and security. The recollection of that frightening night is so potent that it overshadows even the happiest times with a shadow of unease. Her husband has noticed these changes in Mrs. Lin’s behavior over time. She avoids going out alone and often checks every corner of their home for signs of breach. This constant threat monitoring has taken a toll on her work as well, where she is often distracted by intrusive thoughts and finds it difficult to focus on tasks that once came naturally. The fear of the unknown stalker has become all-consuming, driving Mrs. Lin to seek help finally. She had come to believe that no place was truly safe for her anymore. The most significant catalyst for seeking therapy was an incident at work where she became visibly distressed during a routine maintenance check, unable to focus and feeling overwhelmed by the memories resurfacing. In therapy, Mrs. Lin is most afraid of reliving those terrifying moments but simultaneously hopes for relief from the relentless hypervigilance that has taken over her life. She longs for a sense of safety and normalcy, wishing to reclaim the peace she once felt in both her home and workplace. Despite the challenges, she remains determined to regain control over her daily life and find solace in understanding and managing her trauma.
